judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 5036. It would make fertility fraud a crime. Knowingly giving false or misleading information about the embryo, egg or sperm used in assisted reproduction, or about a donor's identity or medical history, would be a felony punishable by up to 5 years in prison or a $50,000 fine. A health professional who knowingly or recklessly used an embryo, egg or sperm other than the one the patient agreed to in writing, including the professional's own, would face up to 15 years or a $100,000 fine. The House passed it 60-49. The Senate has not voted on it, so it is not law.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against House Bill 5036. It would make fertility fraud a crime. A health professional who knowingly or recklessly used an embryo, egg or sperm other than the one the patient agreed to in writing, including the professional's own, would face up to 15 years or a $100,000 fine. judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 5037. It would set the time limit for charging the new fertility fraud crime at 15 years. If DNA evidence points to an unidentified person, charges could be filed at any time, and within 15 years after that person is identified. The House passed it 61-48. The Senate has not voted on it, so it is not law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 5035. It would let people harmed by fertility fraud sue for three times their damages plus lawyer fees. The patient who gave birth, the patient's spouse at the time, a person conceived through the fraud, and the donor could all sue, with a separate claim for each child born. A suit would have to be filed within 3 years after the fraud is discovered. The House passed it 61-48. The Senate has not voted on it, so it is not law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 5574. It would make it a crime to ignore a first responder's spoken warning to stay back and to come and stay within 25 feet with the intent to interfere with, threaten or harass the responder. It would carry up to 60 days in jail or a $500 fine, up to 2 years if it injures the responder, and up to 15 years if it causes the responder's death. First responders would include police, corrections officers, firefighters and emergency medical workers. The House passed it 74-30. The Senate has not voted on it, so it is not law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 5744. It would make it a felony to shoot on purpose at a vehicle the shooter knows or has reason to believe is occupied, punishable by up to 10 years in prison or a $10,000 fine. If the shooter knows or has reason to believe a child is inside, the penalty would be up to 20 years or a $20,000 fine. The House passed it 79-24. The Senate has not voted on it, so it is not law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 5652. It would bar people who own or live on property within 5 miles of a motor racing track from suing the track over nuisance, a taking of property, or any other theory, if the track was there before they bought or built. The shield would stay in place even if the track later changed its size, layout, technology or type of racing, as long as the changes are lawful. Tracks would still have to follow environmental and health and safety laws. The House passed it 64-38. The Senate has not voted on it, so it is not law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 4949. It would widen the shield that protects sport shooting ranges from noise lawsuits and noise-related prosecution. Today a range is protected if it follows accepted practices and met the noise rules in place when it opened. The protection would continue even after the range is updated, modified or expanded, as long as the changes follow accepted practices. The House passed it 56-51. The Senate has not voted on it, so it is not law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 4582. It would write into law the rule that a property owner or occupant owes business visitors no duty to protect them from, or warn them of, dangers that are open and obvious. The Michigan Supreme Court dropped that rule in 2023. A narrow exception would remain for dangers that are effectively unavoidable or pose an unreasonably high risk of severe harm, and courts could not adopt a broader reasonable-care standard. The House passed it 58-48. The Senate has not voted on it, so it is not law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 5298. It would change who pays no-fault injury benefits when a passenger is hurt in a limousine or in a charter or other bus not already covered by the current rules. The passenger's own auto insurance would pay first, instead of the vehicle's insurer, unless the passenger has no other policy. The House passed it 67-40. The Senate has not voted on it, so it is not law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 4933. It would repeal Michigan's licensing of personnel agencies, the employment and career counseling businesses that charge job seekers a fee, and of the agents who manage them. These businesses would no longer need a state license to operate. The House passed it 57-46. The Senate has not voted on it, so it is not law.
